TITLE: SNP members back resolution supporting UK-wide ban on X | The Independent
PUBLISHED: 2026-10-17T12:52:08.000Z  MODIFIED: 2026-10-17T12:52:08.000Z


BookmarkBookmark popoverRemoved from bookmarks


A motion in support of a UK-wide ban of the social media platform X has been backed by the SNP – with party members also calling for the Scottish Government and Holyrood authorities to remove themselves from the site.

SNP members at the party’s annual conference in Aberdeen overwhelmingly passed a resolution stressing the need for “responsible  use of social media”.

It insisted the SNP, elected representatives, councils, the Scottish Government and other public bodies, should “not make use of harmful platforms that harbour abusive content”.

Following the debate an SNP spokesperson confirmed: “As per the motion passed by conference, we will review our use of X and report to the party’s national executive.”

Formerly known as Twitter, X was acquired by the billionaire Elon Musk in 2022, with the platform now owned by SpaceX’s artificial intelligence subsidiary SpaceXAI.

Moving the resolution, SNP member Erin Lux insisted: “There are so many reasons we need to remove ourselves and our services from this platform”.

The party has almost 320,000 followers on X and regularly posts on the platform, including several updates from the conference in recent days.

But Ms Lux claimed that X and its artificial intelligence chatbot Grok “continue to host and produce child sexual abuse material”, going on to state that X is a “hotbed of mis- and disinformation”.

Adding that research had showed using the platform “shifted views rightwards”, Ms Lux asked delegates: “Why on earth are we continuing to post there?”

She insisted: “It is indefensible we are lending our credibility as a party, and the credibility of our elected officials to a site that has become a hotbed of misinformation and abuse.

“Do we really want our party messaging appearing alongside nudified images of our fellow politicians?

“Do we think it is acceptable to force people to log into a site that shares child sexual abuse material to find out if the trains are back on?

“Is it really in our interests to keep driving traffic towards a right wing radicalisation machine?”

Adding that there was a “growing consensus” in favour of leaving the platform, she told fellow SNP members: “We need to show moral strength and the courage of our convictions and choose to use social media responsibly in a way that aligns with our values.”

Fellow SNP member David Birkett argued against a ban, saying he could “understand why people don’t like” the platform, but the party should remain active on it because of it has larger user numbers than rival social media sites.

He told the conference: “Bluesky has 10.4 million active monthly users, X has 551 million. Bluesky has three million daily active users, X has 251 million.

Mr Birkett continued: “I also believe in treating party bodies, candidates and elected members like grown-ups, who can make their own assessment of which platforms they choose to join without some edict.”

He highlighted the role X can play in informing travellers about delays and disruptions to ferries, train services and on the roads.

Mr Birkett said: “Maybe one day Bluesky and others will have the reach that X does and we can rethink this. But until it does, we should keep the party, the Government, the Parliament and other public bodies on the platform.”
